chunks: A man said to him: 'I went out to Makkah, so a man accompanied me and he was my travel companion. When we were on one of the roads, he fell ill and became severely burdened. I used to take care of him. Then he regained consciousness to the extent that there was no problem with him in my estimation. When the day came in which he died, he regained consciousness, then died on that very day.'

So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'There is not a dying person upon whom death presents itself except that God, Mighty and Majestic, restores to him his hearing, his eyesight, and his intellect for the bequest — whether he makes the bequest or neglects it. And it is the comfort that is called 'the comfort of death', and it is a right upon every Muslim.'

key_terms.الوصية: The bequest/will — the Islamic legal obligation to specify how one's affairs and estate should be handled after death
key_terms.الوفاة: Death/dying — the process of passing away, used here to describe the moment when death presents itself
key_terms.راحة الموت: The 'comfort of death' — the transient return of awareness and lucidity experienced by the dying, explained here as a Divine gift enabling the fulfillment of wasiyya

ai.seo_question: Why do dying people sometimes regain consciousness before death in Islam?
ai.summary: A man recounts to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) that his travel companion to Makkah became gravely ill and seemed to recover before dying on the same day of his apparent recovery. The Imam explains that this momentary lucidity is a Divine mercy: God restores the faculties of every dying person so they may fulfill the obligation of making a bequest (wasiyya). The Imam identifies this phenomenon as 'the comfort of death' (rahat al-mawt) and declares it a universal right and obligation for every Muslim — grounding a personal observation in a fundamental rule of Islamic jurisprudence regarding the duty of making a will.
word_analysis: comes to him/presents itself to him

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hamaad Bin Usman, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, ‘A man said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘I went out to Makkah, so a man accompanied me, and he was my colleague. So when we were in one of the roads, he fell sick and slackened with intense slackness. I used to take care of him. Then he woke up to the extent that there was no problem with him in my presence. So when it was the day in which he died, he was awake, and he died during that day’.

So Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘There is no dying one and the death presents itself except that Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Mighty and Majestic Restores to him, his hearing, and his eyesight, and his mind for the bequest. He either takes to the bequeathing or neglects it, and it is the comfort which is called ‘the comfort of death’. So it is a right upon every Muslim (to leave a bequest)’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from Hammad ibn ‘Uthaman who has narrated the following: “Once, a man said to abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, ‘I once travelled to Makkah and my travel mate, who was a friend, on the way became ill very seriously and I looked after him. He began to feel very well and I thought he is fine. On the day that he died, he became extremely well but on the same day, he died.’

Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, said, ‘To anyone who is about to die, Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious, returns his hearing, seeing and reasoning abilities so that he can make a will, regardless of whether he makes a will or not. It is the comfort that is called the comfort of death and that is the right of every Muslim.’”
